entities.name: Phaedrus the Epicurean
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Phaedrus, a distinguished Epicurean philosopher, held the esteemed position of scholarch, or head, of the Epicurean school in Athens from approximately 75 BCE until his death in 69 BCE. He played a crucial role in the transmission and interpretation of Epicurean doctrine during a pivotal period when Roman intellectuals were increasingly engaging with Greek philosophy. His significance lies not only in his leadership of the Athenian school but also in his direct personal influence on prominent Roman figures, most notably the orator and statesman Marcus Tullius Cicero, thereby shaping the Roman reception of Epicurean thought.

Phaedrus's career saw him engage deeply with the philosophical currents of his time, advocating for the Epicurean emphasis on pleasure as the highest good, understood as freedom from pain and mental disturbance (ataraxia). His association with Cicero began in Rome during Cicero's youth, where the aspiring orator studied under him. Later, during Cicero's residence in Athens, he renewed this acquaintance, finding Phaedrus as an aging but still vibrant intellectual leader. Phaedrus, alongside other notable Epicureans like Philodemus, was instrumental in maintaining the intellectual vitality of the Garden in Athens, ensuring the continuity of its teachings amidst evolving philosophical landscapes. He was also a close friend and intellectual mentor to Velleius, another Roman whose views on Epicureanism were articulated through Cicero's dialogues.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Phaedrus's leadership of the Epicurean school and his direct influence on key Roman figures like Cicero were crucial for the transmission of Epicurean philosophy into Roman intellectual life, shaping its understanding for centuries.
